The oxidizing agent is the species that is reduced (it gains electrons) in the redox reaction.
Assign oxidation states: S in H2S is −2 and Cl in Cl2 is 0; in the products S is 0 (S(s)) and Cl is −1 (in HCl).
Because S goes from −2 to 0 it loses electrons and is oxidized, so H2S acts as the reducing agent, not the oxidizing agent.
Cl2 goes from 0 to −1 (each chlorine atom gains one electron) and is therefore reduced, so Cl2 is the oxidizing agent — the correct option.
Elemental sulfur (S) is the oxidized product and cannot be the oxidizing agent, while HCl is the reduced product containing chloride ions produced by reduction of Cl2.
Electron balance shows each S atom loses two electrons which are accepted by chlorine (Cl2 + 2e− → 2Cl−), confirming Cl2 accepts electrons and oxidizes H2S.

Le Chatelier’s principle describes how an equilibrium responds to changes in temperature, pressure and concentrations.
The given reaction is exothermic (ΔH = −90 kJ), so heat behaves like a product of the forward reaction.
Increasing temperature supplies extra heat and therefore shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants (left), decreasing the yield of NH3.
A catalyst does not change the equilibrium position; it only speeds up the attainment of equilibrium, so the NH3 yield is unchanged.
Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gaseous moles (2 mol NH3 vs 4 mol on the reactant side), so pressure increase would raise, not lower, NH3 yield.
Removing ammonia shifts the equilibrium to the right to produce more NH3, thus removal increases the yield rather than decreases it.

This question checks which functional group behaves as a Bronsted acid strong enough to react with bicarbonate to give CO2.
Alkanoic acids (carboxylic acids, RCOOH) donate H+ to HCO3− to form RCOO− and H2CO3, and H2CO3 decomposes to CO2 and H2O: RCOOH + NaHCO3 → RCOONa + CO2 + H2O.
An alkanoate is the deprotonated carboxylate salt (RCOO−), so it will not liberate CO2 with NaHCO3 because no acidic proton is available.
Alkanones (ketones) lack the acidic carboxyl hydrogen and therefore do not react with NaHCO3 to produce effervescence.
Amines are basic (not acidic) and may be protonated by strong acids but do not give CO2 when treated with NaHCO3.
Hence Alkanoic Acid is correct: only carboxylic acids among the options react with bicarbonate to evolve CO2.

2-methylpropanoic acid has a three‑carbon propanoic acid backbone with a methyl substituent on C‑2 (common name: isobutyric acid).
The condensed structural formula (CH₃)₂CHCOOH explicitly shows two methyl groups attached to the second carbon of the propanoyl chain and therefore represents 2‑methylpropanoic acid.
Counting atoms in (CH₃)₂CHCOOH gives the molecular formula C₄H₈O₂ (4 C, 8 H, 2 O).
CH₃(CH₂)₃COOH is a five‑carbon straight‑chain carboxylic acid (pentanoic acid) and does not match a C₄ skeleton.
CH₃(CH₂)₂COOH is unbranched butanoic acid; it has the same molecular formula C₄H₈O₂ but is a structural isomer, not the branched 2‑methylpropanoic structure.
CH₃CH₂COOH is propanoic acid (three carbons) and lacks the extra methyl group required for 2‑methylpropanoic acid.

CH3CH2COOC2H5 is the ester ethyl propanoate (ethyl propionate).
Esters are formed by acid‑catalysed condensation of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol: RCOOH + R'OH → RCOOR' + H2O.
In CH3CH2COOC2H5 the acyl part CH3CH2CO– comes from propanoic acid (CH3CH2COOH) and the alkyl part C2H5– comes from ethanol (C2H5OH), so propanoic acid + ethanol is the correct reactant pair.
Ethanoic acid + propanol would produce propyl ethanoate (CH3COOC3H7), not the given ester.
Propanoic acid + propanol would produce propyl propanoate (CH3CH2COOC3H7), and ethanoic acid + ethanol would give ethyl ethanoate (CH3COOC2H5); both are different structures.
Therefore the correct choice is Propanoic acid + Ethanol because it supplies the CH3CH2CO– and C2H5– fragments that match CH3CH2COOC2H5.

Detergents are surfactants composed of a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail and a hydrophilic head that together lower surface tension and solubilize oils.
Using straight (linear) hydrocarbon chains makes the hydrophobic tails less sterically hindered and more accessible to microbial enzymes, so they biodegrade more readily.
Linear alkylbenzene sulfonates (LAS) are a standard example: linear chains were adopted because they break down in sewage treatment more efficiently than branched chains.
Solubility is primarily controlled by the polar head group and the overall hydrophile–lipophile balance, not merely by whether the tail is straight or branched, although tail length also matters.
Foaming depends on the surfactant class and formulation (air entrapment, additives), so high foam is not guaranteed by straight chains alone.
Alkalinity describes pH or added basic agents in the formulation and is unrelated to the geometry of the hydrocarbon tail, so 'alkaline' is not the reason for straight chains.

Fractional distillation separates crude oil into lighter and heavier fractions by boiling point, leaving a dense heavy residue at the bottom.
The heavy residual fraction is commonly called bitumen or asphalt and is solid or semi-solid at ambient temperature.
Bitumen is used as coatings for pipes because it provides waterproofing, adhesion and resistance to corrosion and weathering.
Tractor fuel is obtained from the diesel or gas-oil fraction (middle distillates), not from the heavy residue.
Aviation fuels are kerosene-range fractions (jet fuel) with properties unsuitable for the heavy residual and so are not made from bitumen.
Some heavy residues can be upgraded by cracking, but the unprocessed residual solids are primarily used as asphaltic coatings rather than as aviation or tractor fuels.

An acid anhydride undergoes nucleophilic acyl substitution because the carbonyl carbons are electrophilic and are attacked by ammonia.
Ammonia replaces one acyl group to form an amide (RCONH2) while the other acyl fragment becomes a carboxylic acid or its ammonium salt, so the organic nitrogen product is an amide.
Therefore option D (Amides) is correct as the direct organic product of anhydride + NH3.
Amines (option A) are nitrogen-containing bases but would require reduction or deacylation to form from an anhydride, not simple reaction with NH3.
Amino acids (option B) have both -NH2 and -COOH on the same carbon and are not produced by treating a generic acid anhydride with NH3 under normal conditions.
Ethanoate (option C) denotes an acetate ion or ester fragment and is not the nitrogen-containing organic product expected, so it is incorrect.

An alkanone is a ketone (R2C=O) and reduction supplies hydrogen to the carbonyl group.
LiAlH4 is a strong hydride donor that delivers H- to the carbonyl carbon and subsequent protonation yields an alcohol.
When a ketone is reduced the carbon bearing two alkyl groups becomes R2CH–OH, which is a secondary alkanol.
Thus the correct option is Secondary alkanols because ketones give secondary alcohols on reduction while aldehydes give primary alcohols.
Polyhydric (multiple‑OH) alkanols arise only if the substrate has more than one reducible group or multiple carbonyls, not from a single ketone.
Tertiary alcohols are not formed by direct hydride reduction of a carbonyl because forming a tertiary alcohol would require creating a new C–C bond or breaking an alkyl–carbon bond, not simply adding hydrogen.

Destructive distillation of coal involves heating coal strongly in the absence of air so that volatile products are driven off and a solid residue remains.
The non‑volatile solid left behind is coke — a hard, porous, carbon‑rich material produced when volatiles (coal gas, coal tar, ammoniacal liquor) are removed.
Coke has high fixed carbon and little volatile matter because thermal decomposition converts organic constituents to gases and liquids, leaving a carbon matrix.
Because of its strength, porosity and high carbon content coke is used as a fuel and as a reducing agent in blast furnaces.
Coal tar and coal gas are volatile condensates (liquid and gas respectively) collected during destructive distillation, while lamp black is soot from incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons and not the distillation residue.
Hence the correct non‑volatile residue from destructive distillation of coal is coke.

N₂O is a colorless, sweet‑smelling gas that produces analgesia and mild general anaesthesia and is widely used in dentistry and short procedures.
Its anaesthetic action comes from CNS depression when inhaled at suitable concentrations, often in combination with other agents.
NO₂ (nitrogen dioxide) is a reddish‑brown, strongly oxidizing and irritating gas that is toxic to the respiratory tract, not an anaesthetic.

NO (nitric oxide) can be used medically as an inhaled vasodilator in specific respiratory situations but is not an inhalational anaesthetic like N₂O.

Alkaline pyrogallol absorbs oxygen because pyrogallol is readily oxidized in alkaline solution, removing O2 from an air stream.
Caustic potash (KOH) absorbs carbon dioxide by converting CO2 into potassium carbonate/bicarbonate, so CO2 is removed.
Hence the constituents removed are O2 and CO2 when air is passed successively through alkaline pyrogallol and caustic potash.
Nitrogen is not removed because neither reagent reacts appreciably with N2 under these conditions, so N2 remains in the residual gas.
Options that merely reverse the order (CO2 & O2) or repeat O2 & CO2 state the same constituents; the order in the option does not change which gases are absorbed.
Confidence: high; these conclusions follow standard senior-secondary chemistry: pyrogallol absorbs O2 and KOH absorbs CO2.

The question distinguishes forms of iron by carbon content and their mechanical properties, especially tensile strength.
Cast iron contains about 2–4% carbon, making it hard and brittle with relatively low tensile strength, so it is the correct choice for objects that do not require high tensile strength.
Cast iron is used for castings such as pipes, manhole covers, stoves and other items where castability and compressive strength matter more than tensile strength.
Pig iron is the crude blast-furnace product with very high carbon and impurities and is generally an intermediate material rather than a finished product for making objects.
Wrought iron has very low carbon, is malleable and tough with good tensile strength, and is used where ductility and strength are required.
Iron rust (iron oxide) is a flaky, non-metallic corrosion product and is not a usable metallic form for manufacturing objects.

Aqua regia is a mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the volumetric ratio 3:1 (HCl:HNO3).
Nitric acid serves as the oxidizing agent while hydrochloric acid supplies chloride ions that form stable chloro‑complexes with oxidized metal ions, allowing gold and platinum to dissolve.
The reaction mixture also produces reactive species such as chlorine (Cl2) and nitrosyl chloride (NOCl) that assist the oxidation process.
A 3:1 ratio balances oxidizing power and chloride availability so oxidized metal stays solubilized as complexes (for example AuCl4−).
Alternative ratios like 1:1 or 2:1 provide less chloride and so weaker complexation, while 1:3 has excess oxidizer but insufficient chloride to form stable metal‑chloride complexes, which is why 3:1 is standard.
Concentrated acids and aqua regia are highly corrosive and reactive, so preparation and handling require appropriate laboratory safety measures.

Tartaric acid is a naturally occurring dicarboxylic acid (2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid) found in certain fruits and plants.
Grapes, particularly wine grapes, are a well-known and significant source of tartaric acid and this acid influences wine acidity and stability.

Remembering typical fruit acids helps distinguish options: grapes → tartaric acid, citrus fruits → citric acid, and many pomes (e.g., apples) → malic acid.

The hydrogen ion H+ has no electrons and cannot contribute an electron pair to form a normal covalent bond.
Oxygen in H2O carries two lone pairs; one lone pair is donated to H+ to form the hydronium ion H3O+ (H2O + H+ → H3O+).
This donation creates a coordinate (dative) covalent bond, meaning both bonding electrons come from the oxygen atom.
The O–H bond in H3O+ is covalent in bonding character but is described as dative because of the one‑sided electron donation.
It is not ionic because no full electron transfer produces separate charged species, and it is not metallic because no metal atoms or delocalised metallic bonding are involved.
Therefore the best answer is “Dative”; the plain option “Covalent” is related but less precise, while “Ionic” and “Metallic” are incorrect.

Electrical conductivity of aqueous solutions depends on the concentration of ions and the degree to which the solute ionizes.
Strong electrolytes such as HCl ionize essentially completely, whereas weak electrolytes like ethanoic (acetic) acid ionize only partially.
A 2.0 M HCl solution therefore supplies the largest concentration of charge carriers (H+ and Cl−), and the very high mobility of H+ further increases conductivity.
0.5 M HCl is also a strong acid but at lower concentration it provides fewer ions and so conducts less than 2.0 M HCl.
2.0 M ethanoic acid, although more concentrated, remains a weak acid and produces far fewer ions than 2.0 M HCl, so its conductivity is much lower.
0.5 M ethanoic acid is both dilute and weakly ionized, making it the least conducting option here.

Ionization energy is the energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom and depends mainly on nuclear charge, atomic radius and electron shielding.
Fluorine has a small atomic radius and a relatively high effective nuclear charge on its valence electrons, so those electrons are held more tightly and require more energy to remove.
Potassium's outer electron is in a much larger orbital (4s) and is strongly shielded by inner electrons, so it is held less tightly and has a much lower ionization energy.
Thus the option "Nuclear charge & atomic size" correctly explains why fluorine's ionization energy is far higher than potassium's.
Mass, density and melting point are bulk or material properties and do not directly determine the first ionization energy of isolated atoms.
Atomic mass can correlate with size in a general sense but is not the controlling factor for ionization energy, so the other options are not plausible explanations for the observed difference.

Enthalpy change (ΔH) measures heat absorbed or released by a reaction at constant pressure.
A positive ΔH means the reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings, so it is endothermic.
Endothermic processes include melting, vaporization, and photosynthesis where heat is taken into the system.
The opposite is exothermic, which has negative ΔH and releases heat to the surroundings; therefore 'Exothermic' is incorrect.
Spontaneity depends on Gibbs free energy (ΔG = ΔH - TΔS), so a positive ΔH does not by itself determine whether a reaction is spontaneous.
'Neutral' is not a standard thermochemical classification for ΔH; reactions with ΔH ≈ 0 have negligible heat exchange but are not typically called neutral.
